chunks: "An MMU is the hardware block between the CPU and memory that translates virtual addresses into physical addresses and checks permissions on every access.
Programs don't see real RAM addresses. Each process gets its own virtual address space, divided into pages, usually 4 KB.
The OS keeps a page table per process that says which physical frame each virtual page maps to and whether it's readable, writable or executable.
On each load or store the MMU looks up the translation, mostly in a small cache called the TLB, and if it's not there it walks the page table in memory. Why do we need it?
First, isolation and protection: one process can't touch another's memory or the kernel's, and a bad pointer becomes a page fault instead of corrupting the system.
Second, convenience: every program can pretend it has a big contiguous address space starting at the same address, while the OS scatters its pages across physical RAM wherever there's room.
Third, it enables demand paging and swapping, memory-mapped files and shared libraries that share physical pages between processes.
The cost is extra latency and area, which is why there's a TLB. Small microcontrollers skip it and use at most an MPU for protection, which keeps them simple and deterministic."
